newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia police track suspicious drug money trail.
newsitem.headline: Colombia police track suspicious drug money trail.

text.p: A huge cache of drug money linked to a Cali cartel kingpin may provide the hardest evidence yet for longstanding U.S. charges that drug lords are trafficking narcotics from inside Colombia's prisons.

Nearly $5 million in suspected cocaine cash was discovered by police on Tuesday in a raid on a house in the southwest city of Cali, most of it in $100 and $50 bills sealed in wrappers marked "Reserva Federal Bank," an apparent reference to the U.S. Federal Reserve.

National Police chief Rosso Jose Serrano, in a lengthy interview with Radionet news radio on Wednesday, charged that the money belonged to Helmer "El Pacho" Herrera, No. 4 man in the Cali drug mob, who surrendered to police last September.

Herrera's personal fortune has been estimated by Semana, Colombia's leading news magazine, at $11 billion and he is the target of an extradition request by U.S. Attorney General Janet Reno made while he was still at large last summer.

The United States has said repeatedly that top Cali drug bosses, most of whom were arrested in 1995, continue running their empire from jail. Washington has offered little evidence to support that charge but cited it as one reason for last month's decision to keep Colombia on a drugs blacklist because of its alleged failure to crack down hard enough on narcotics.

Serrano said one of the most alarming things about the drug money linked to Herrera -- apart from the fact that it may have come from a U.S. Federal Reserve bank -- was that some of the bills were issued less than two weeks ago. "The last few packets of dollars are dated Feb. 28 of this year. That's something that has me a little bit worried," he said.

Feb. 28 was the same day the U.S. State Department announced that Colombia had been "decertified" for a second consecutive year because it had failed to prove itself a trusthworthy ally in the war on drugs.

Asked if the cash meant Herrera was still trafficking from inside the maximum security wing of the Palmira prison outside Cali, Serrano said that was something he could not rule out. "We don't know if this was a late payment for drugs or if the frontmen for these guys (cartel kingpins) are still in business," he told the radio network.

"It's something we're going to establish," he added when pressed for his personal opinion as to whether the discovery of the cash, some of it in brand new $100 bills, indicated that Herrera was still flooding the U.S. market with drugs.

"It is very suspicious," he said, adding that he had asked U.S. Ambassador Myles Frechette for help in tracing the money through serial numbers to find out "where it came from and where it was supposed to go." The U.S. Embassy had no immediate comment.

Serrano told Reuters in a telephone interview from Cali on Tuesday that the cash totalled about $4.8 million. In his interview with Radionet, he said police intelligence agents had determined that the last instalment of the cash entered Cali in the hands of an unidentified courier who flew into the city's international airport on Monday night.

"Dollars are made over there and not here," Serrano said, referring to the United States. "They (the U.S.) have to help us control the movement of money," he added. "The bottom line of the drug trade is money but we need help controlling it because payments are made in dollars not (Colombian) pesos."
